To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) interactions are not a property of data, but rather of the model used to describe it; (2) interactions can be quantified as the difference between the best approximation to a joint probability distribution and the best approximation that does not admit that there are interactions; (3) most machine learning procedures fail to capture interactions, which is why they often produce poor models; (4) the best way to present interactions is by showing how well a joint probability distribution can be approximated without admitting that

interactions are a) the most interesting patterns in data that b) are not treated appropriately by machine learning procedures, and that c) are quantified by how well we can model a joint probability distribution.

1) the notion of an interaction in statistics and in machine learning is different; 2) interactions can be quantified; 3) interactions are ubiquitous and important; and 4) interactions are usually not taken into account by machine learning algorithms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
quantifying, visualizing and modeling interactions in data, and with the consequences of ignoring interactions for machine learning algorithms.
